source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Founding retrieval-plus-ensemble LLM forecaster. Pipeline: LM writes search queries (plus sub-question queries), news APIs return articles, a cheap LM rates relevance and summarizes, a reasoning LM writes forecasts, forecasts are aggregated. Test set only has questions opened after the models' cutoff.
numbers: 5 platforms; 5,516 binary questions (3,762 train, 840 val, 914 test); 7.17M human forecasts in raw data. Test Brier: system 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 vs best no-retrieval baseline GPT-4-1106 0.208 (zero-shot); accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%.
quote: On average, the system nears the crowd aggregate of competitive forecasters, and in some settings surpasses it.
limits: Brier SEs assume iid, so likely too small. Retrieval dates simulated with date-filtered news APIs (see leakage papers c10, c11). Hyperparameters tuned on validation, not live.
agent_relevance: Template for S3: query expansion, relevance filter, summarize, several independent reasoning runs, then robust average.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Out of the box, models are poor forecasters without retrieval. 14 LMs tested zero-shot and scratchpad; most are near or worse than the 0.25 coin-flip score. Only the GPT-4 and Claude-2 families beat it by more than 0.02.
numbers: Test Brier zero-shot / scratchpad: GPT-4-1106 0.208/0.209; Claude-2.1 0.220/0.215; Gemini-Pro 0.243/0.230; Llama-2-13B 0.226/0.268; Mixtral 0.238/0.238. Human crowd 0.149.
limits: Models of 2023-24; frontier models since have moved (see c12, c19).
agent_relevance: A single no-search pass is weak. Retrieval and aggregation are needed, not optional.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Retrieval ablation. Removing retrieval hurts a lot; fine-tuning matters less. Full system with 6 forecasts (3 base GPT-4 prompts + 3 fine-tuned samples at T=0.5) is best.
numbers: Ablation test Brier (system alone): full 0.179; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 + base GPT-4 0.182; base GPT-4 only 0.181; base GPT-4 with no IR 0.186; no retrieval and no fine-tuned model 0.206. Retrieval alone is worth about 0.02 Brier (0.206 to 0.186).
limits: Single study, one retrieval stack; SE about 0.002-0.003 so the 0.179 vs 0.181 gaps are within noise.
agent_relevance: Most of the lift comes from retrieved context, not from clever training. Spend the budget on search quality.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Ensemble method comparison (Appendix E.1). Five aggregators on 6 base reasonings. Trimmed mean was best, but gaps between mean, median and geometric mean are tiny. Universal self-consistency (an LM reads all runs and writes one answer) did NOT beat no ensembling.
numbers: Validation Brier: trimmed mean 0.1649; median 0.1651; geometric mean 0.1655; mean 0.1656; no ensemble 0.1676; USC 0.1691; human crowd 0.1600. So averaging 6 runs gains only about 0.0027 over one run.
limits: Their trimmed mean is nonstandard: half-weights the forecast farthest from the median. Ensemble members are correlated (same model, same retrieved articles).
agent_relevance: S3: average independent runs with code (mean or trimmed), do not let an LLM judge merge them. Expect a small gain (about 0.003), larger when runs are more independent.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Where the system beats the crowd, and crowd adjustment. System beat crowd when crowd was unsure (0.3-0.7), at early retrieval dates, and with 5+ relevant articles. Averaging system and crowd beat either alone in every row.
numbers: Crowd in 0.3-0.7 (val): system 0.199 vs crowd 0.246. Test, all three conditions: system 0.240 vs crowd 0.247 (22% of forecasts). Combined with crowd (4x weight on crowd, tuned on val): test Brier 0.149 to 0.146, a gain of 0.003. Hedging: system worse by 0.04 Brier when crowd is within 0.05 of 0 or 1, though 7% more accurate.
quote: our system outperforms the crowd when the crowd's predictions express high uncertainty
limits: Crowd gain is about 0.003 here; the 'nearly 0.01' figure in the SUBFIELDS row was not found in this paper and is not verified. Selective forecasting uses hindsight-tuned heuristics.
agent_relevance: Use an external anchor (market or crowd price) when it exists, weight it heavily; model adds most where the anchor is near 50%. Safety-trained hedging toward the middle costs Brier on easy questions.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy (Science Advances 2025)
finding: Study 1. Median of 12 different LLMs (no retrieval) versus the 925-person human crowd on a 3-month tournament. Preregistered test: LLM crowd beats the no-information benchmark and is not different from the human crowd.
numbers: 31 binary questions. LLM-crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850. vs 0.25 benchmark: t(30)=-2.35, p=0.026. Equivalence within a 0.081 Brier bound: p=0.017 and p=0.040. Model differences exist, F(12,354)=2.64, p=0.002.
quote: the LLM crowd outperforms a simple no-information benchmark and is not statistically different from the human crowd
limits: Only 31 questions; 14 resolved Yes. Wide equivalence bound.
agent_relevance: Diversity across models gives a crowd effect even without search. Cheap evidence for S3 using different model families, not only repeated samples.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Acquiescence bias. LLM forecasts lean toward Yes even though outcomes split nearly evenly. Averaging many models does not remove a shared bias.
numbers: Median model forecast 60%, range 0.1% to 99.5%. Mean forecast 57.35% (SD 20.93), above 50% with p<0.001. Only 14 of 31 questions resolved Yes.
limits: Small question set. Bias may differ in other question mixes (c05 found hedging to the middle instead).
agent_relevance: Ensembling cuts noise, not shared bias. Add a base-rate check and a flip-the-question check before the average.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (Study 2)
finding: Crowd adjustment test. Showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median prediction improves their Brier, but simply averaging the model forecast with the human median is better than the models' own updated forecast.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003). Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001). Accuracy gain 17% to 28%. Simple model-human average beat updates: GPT-4 0.13 (t(92)=2.583, p=.011), Claude 2 0.14 (t(92)=3.530, p=.001). Model shift correlates with gap size, r=0.88 and r=0.87.
limits: Human median came from the same tournament; single study, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: When an outside crowd number exists, average it in with code. Letting the LLM reason about it adds nothing over the arithmetic.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: Preregistered RCT. Humans with a GPT-4-Turbo assistant gave better forecasts than a control group with a weaker assistant; even an overconfident, base-rate-neglecting assistant helped.
numbers: N=991, 6 questions. Accuracy gain 24% to 28% vs control. Without outlier question 3: superforecasting assistant +41%, noisy assistant +29%. Aggregate (mean-of-medians) Brier: superforecast-assistant 0.52, noisy 0.41, control 0.55 (all questions); excluding Q3: 0.11, 0.28, 0.15. No consistent harm to crowd diversity.
limits: One outlier item drives much of the effect. Control was a weaker LLM, not no LLM. Noisy assistant improved the aggregate with all questions but looked worse than control once Q3 was excluded.
agent_relevance: Human-side evidence that LLM advice is useful but noisy; supports keeping an external check in the loop on the aggregate.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping, Tramer (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Retrospective (backtest) forecasts are hard to trust. Leakage comes from answer-revealing questions, date-filtered search that still returns future pages, and retrievers trained on later data. Also logical leakage: questions that only resolved early.
numbers: At least 3.8% of the Halawi test set resolved early (no forecast needed); at least 10% of Tao et al. 2025 questions trivial by resolve date. Weak classifiers reach over 80% on binary news-generated questions of Dai et al. 2025; a DeBERTa classifier gets 55% on a 4-choice set with 25% chance (Metaculus 55%, Manifold 59%). Over 90% of Dai et al. questions judged unrealistically specific (subjective).
quote: difficulty in trusting evaluation results due to many forms of temporal leakage
limits: Position paper with spot audits, not a full replication of Halawi.
agent_relevance: Any score we measure for our agent with web search must be on live, unresolved questions or a frozen corpus. Retrieval gain numbers from backtests are upper bounds.

source: El Lahib, Xia, Li, Wang, Pi (2026) Temporal Leakage in Search-Engine Date-Filtered Web Retrieval: A Retrospective Forecasting Case Study
finding: Direct audit of date-filtered web search used in retrospective forecasting. Google before: filter and DuckDuckGo date-range both leak post-cutoff pages (updated articles, related-content boxes, wrong metadata, absence signals).
numbers: At least one major-leak page for 71% of questions (Google) and 81% (DuckDuckGo); answer directly revealed for 41% and 55%. With gpt-oss-120b, Brier 0.10 with leaky documents vs 0.24 with leak-free documents (0.24 is near coin-flip level).
quote: date-restricted search on these engines is insufficient for credible retrospective evaluation
limits: Question count not extracted; one forecasting model.
agent_relevance: Big finding: apparent retrieval gain can be mostly leakage (0.10 vs 0.24). Our evaluation must use time-frozen snapshots or live questions.

source: Hambly, Evans, Schwarz, Phillips (FutureSearch) (2025) Bench to the Future: A Pastcasting Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
finding: Frozen offline web corpus (RetroSearch) with tens of thousands of pages per question to fix the leakage problem. ReAct agent forecasters beat a fixed-evidence pipeline; evidence beats no evidence. Benchmark has 299 questions.
numbers: Single-run variation is large: some questions swing from under 20% to over 80% across runs. Averaging 5 runs cut the standard deviation by about two-thirds. Variable-evidence pipeline SD about 1.7x fixed-evidence, so about 60% of variance came from the final judgment prompt, 40% from information gathering. All no-evidence forecasters still beat 0.25; best (Claude 4) clearly. No significant gain from thinking vs non-thinking models (ReAct).
quote: single forecasts from an LLM should not be considered reliable
limits: Live-vs-retro check on only 20 questions; one retro run missed a decisive live event (NFL Tush Push vote); retro forecasts showed higher variance. Most pairwise model differences not significant. Question set correlated, effective N about 178.8.
agent_relevance: Direct S3 evidence: 5 averaged runs remove about two thirds of run noise. Iterative search (ReAct) beats breadth-first search. Judgment step is the main noise source, so ensemble the judgment, not just the search.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting (RTF)
finding: ReAct agents with search and Python simulation tools, ensembled. Ensembling helps only when each member is already decent: it helped ReAct agents but not base LMs.
numbers: Manifold questions. Brier: crowd 0.172 (acc 73.8%); RTF median of 3 0.169 (72.4%); RTF mean of 3 0.170 (73.9%); RTF single sampled 0.180; Halawi et al. GPT-4o 0.177. Base GPT-4o: ensemble 0.218 vs single 0.210 (ensembling hurt). Ensemble SD 0.092 for ReAct (size 3) vs 0.150 for base LMs (size 4). Calibration index GPT-4o 0.0194 vs ReAct mean 0.0129.
quote: Ensembles only contribute to the final performance if each ensemble member is already sufficiently calibrated.
limits: Small study, small ensembles (3-4), crowd = traded Manifold price, which is a weak crowd.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for S3: averaging only pays when members are better than chance; otherwise it can add variance or bias. Check member quality first.

source: Schneider, Schramm (2025) The Wisdom of Deliberating AI Crowds: Does Deliberation Improve LLM-Based Forecasting?
finding: Letting LLMs read each other's forecasts and update (deliberation) helped only when the group mixed different models and shared information. Same-model groups got no benefit and slightly worse scores. Extra context did not help.
numbers: 202 resolved Metaculus Q2 2025 AI tournament questions; GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini Pro 2.5. Log loss change: diverse+shared -0.020 (0.501 to 0.481, p=0.017, about 4% relative); diverse+distributed -0.022 (p=0.18); homogeneous+distributed +0.008 (p=0.72); homogeneous+shared +0.020 (p=0.14). Median used to aggregate.
limits: One tournament; only the diverse+shared cell is significant; provided information did not improve accuracy, so the information-pooling test failed.
agent_relevance: Same-model self-deliberation gives nothing. Gains need model diversity. For S3 prefer independent runs, and use different model families if available.

source: Chetlapalli, Liao, Chen, Chen (2026) Diverse by Reasoning: Harnessing the Wisdom of LLM Crowds for Future Prediction
finding: Crowd composition can matter more than crowd size. Cluster 25 LLMs by reasoning behavior, pick one medoid per cluster; a 3-model crowd beat voting over all 25 on both benchmarks while using 88% fewer calls and about 80% less cost.
numbers: Pooled held-out, 100 items. FutureX-Past score: medoid voting (K-means++) 0.302; all-25 voting 0.296; performance-picked expert 0.265; random 3 representatives 0.274. BTF-v3: medoid (hierarchical) 0.830, medoid (KM) 0.810, all-25 0.800, expert 0.790. Random same-size crowds match the medoid crowd in about 1 draw in 8.
limits: Score scales differ per benchmark (FutureX-Past is not Brier). Effect belongs to the K-means++ partition; hierarchical medoid was 8th of 10 on FutureX-Past. k=4 dissimilar voting did not transfer. Only 100 items.
agent_relevance: More samples of the same model are redundant. A few diverse reasoners beat many similar ones. Supports few-diverse-runs in S3.

source: Yang, Mahns, Li, Gu, Wu, Xu (2025) LLM-as-a-Prophet: Understanding Predictive Intelligence with Prophet Arena
finding: Live benchmark with a fixed retrieval stage held constant across 23 LLMs. Information sources rank: market data plus news best, none worst. Market data alone is nearly as good; adding news mostly cuts variance. LLMs lag markets near resolution.
numbers: Frontier model Brier falls in a narrow band 0.18-0.22 (random 0.25). Frontier models have about the same Brier as the market baseline but better calibration error and market return. Models with market data only were only slightly worse than with both sources.
quote: slower information aggregation compared to markets when resolution nears
limits: Kalshi prediction-market questions; Brier by condition shown only in a figure, not extracted.
agent_relevance: The best single retrieval item is often an existing aggregate price. Treat market price as anchor, news as variance reducer.

source: Lu, Zhang (2026) The Corroboration Illusion: When More News Makes LLM Forecasts Less True
finding: Boundary condition on retrieval: the forecaster treats retrieved text as truth and ignores provenance. Planted articles in a 17.4M-article Common Crawl News corpus move probabilities a lot, with roughly logarithmic returns to more injected articles.
numbers: ForecastBench questions, n=500 resolved. One LLM-written article flips 56% of forecasts across 0.5; 3 flip 70%, 5 flip 74% (69-73% across forecasters), 10 flip 89%. Net shift +0.13 to +0.22 over a neutral placebo. Brier degraded from 0.18 to 0.37 in the strongest case. Same article labeled as wire service, obscure blog or frequent outlet: shift +0.215, +0.212, +0.214 (provenance ignored). Better-calibrated forecaster with stricter filtering was more vulnerable (flip 74% to 77%).
limits: Small open models (Qwen, Hermes-3-8B) mainly; defenses (publisher lists, isolate-then-aggregate, perplexity filter) each had a cheap bypass.
agent_relevance: Retrieval widens attack surface. Our agent should weigh source reliability explicitly in code and not count repeated near-copies as independent corroboration.

source: Zhang, Stadie (2026) One Fabrication Is Enough: A Fake News Article Changes the Forecasts of LLM Forecasting Systems
finding: One fabricated article, once in context, reverses most opposing forecasts on all frontier models tested. Search-heavy deployed forecasters (multi-run ensembles) are the most exposed because they retrieve it often. Ensembling does not dilute it.
numbers: Reverses 82% of opposing forecasts on stock questions and 74% on prediction-market questions; a genuine article in the same slot changes about one fifth. Deployed agent systems retrieve the fabricated article in about 90% of runs (88-90%) vs 17% for a single retrieval. Defenses: passage filtering and partitioned retrieval each stop one article, together stop four, 16 distorted copies beat them; cost 29% of clean decisions changed, 39% of genuine news discarded, 48 LLM calls vs 1.
limits: Synthetic attack; accuracy barely changes on average because right and wrong directions cancel, so the score hides the harm.
agent_relevance: Averaging 8 runs over the same corpus does not protect against bad sources. Independence must come from separate source sets, not just separate samples.

source: Cao, Du, Chang, Lin, Chen (2026) From Narrative to Auditable Forecasts: A Structured Scaffold for Agentic Forecasting (AuditForecast)
finding: Scaffold: pick a quantitative base model, retrieve only the data it needs (model-guided retrieval) to get a base probability, then apply situational factors as odds multipliers combined by code. Beats narrative-reasoning search agents and some deep-research agents.
numbers: FutureX Brier: GPT-5.4-mini 0.0965 vs Think&Search 0.0970; Gemini-3-flash 0.0675 vs 0.0728. Ablation: model-guided retrieval 11.7 searches and base-probability Brier 0.0802 vs retrieval-then-modeling 23.9 searches and 0.0882. Component ablation Brier: full 0.0764; no scope check 0.0817; no independence check 0.0824; narrative aggregation 0.0815; probability-space aggregation 0.0807.
limits: Mostly value-threshold and market-style questions with a usable quantitative model; gains over Think&Search are small on some backbones.
agent_relevance: Closest match to our schema: arithmetic in code (odds space), explicit independence check, retrieval guided by what the model needs. Halves search cost and improves accuracy.

source: Yuan, Ding, Vlachos (2026) Do Language Models Update their Forecasts with New Information? (EvolveCast)
finding: After new evidence, small open LLMs often move the right direction but by too little, and confidence is badly calibrated against human forecasters' shifts. Giving the whole accumulated news history did not help and often made it worse.
numbers: Directional agreement (MDA) 0.21-0.35 for 1.5B-8B models; magnitude MSE about 0.023-0.027; calibration-change Brier about 0.021-0.025 (negative would be better).
limits: Only 1.5B-8B open models, not frontier; human crowd shifts used as reference, not outcomes.
agent_relevance: Ensemble averaging does not fix under-updating. Use explicit odds-multiplier updating in code (c19) when new evidence arrives.

source: Chi, Chamoun, Ding, Vlachos (2026) WorldReasoner: Evaluating Whether Language Model Agents Forecast Events with Valid Reasoning
finding: Controlled agent settings on 345 resolved tasks with time-gated evidence. Temporally valid retrieval is the strongest driver of accuracy; causal graph reasoning on top does not add accuracy; agents struggle to turn grounded evidence into calibrated probabilities.
numbers: Weighted accuracy over contamination-filtered pairs: Vanilla LLM 58.7%; Causal Simulation 56.6%; Search-Enabled 68.8%; Search-Enabled Graph 64.4%; Near-Resolution 74.7%; Real-Time 88.8% (not reproducible). Key-event recovery 9.8% for Search-Enabled Graph. 345 tasks from 14,141 articles.
limits: Accuracy not Brier; pre-resolution date gates; corpus built by an agentic pipeline.
agent_relevance: Retrieval worth about +10 points accuracy over no retrieval; extra graph structure did not beat plain search. Do not add machinery that does not pay (section 4b).

source: Li, Wang, El Lahib, Xia, Pi (2026, IJCAI) Simulated Ignorance Fails: A Systematic Study of LLM Behaviors on Forecasting Problems Before Model Knowledge Cutoff
finding: Telling a model to ignore what it knows after a date does not work. Cutoff instructions leave a large gap between simulated and true ignorance, chain-of-thought does not suppress prior knowledge, and reasoning-optimized models are worse at it.
numbers: 477 competition-level questions, 9 models. 52% of the pre-cutoff Brier gap remains under simulated ignorance. Share of gap closed by cutoff instructions ranges from 91% (most responsive model) to 28% across models.
limits: Per-model values read from a figure; question set is competition-style.
agent_relevance: Do not evaluate our agent on events the base model may already know; prompting it to forget is not a fix.

source: Paleka, Sudhir, Alvarez, Bhat, et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical consistency of forecasts across related questions (measured by arbitrage profit) predicts true Brier score, so it can score forecasters instantly without waiting for outcomes.
numbers: Consistency metrics correlate positively with Brier on both benchmarks; arbitrage-type checks reach correlation above 0.9 with forecasting performance for tested forecasters, other logical tests give little signal.
limits: Correlation across a small number of forecasters; consistency is necessary, not sufficient for accuracy.
agent_relevance: Cheap S3/S9 check: run an arbitrage test across linked questions in code as a self-quality signal.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench and FRI update posts (search snippet only)
finding: Search result snippets only (full ForecastBench paper opened in subfield 08). An update reports superforecasters at difficulty-adjusted Brier 0.081 and best LLM GPT-4.5 at 0.101, with linear extrapolation putting LLM parity around November 2026 (95% CI Dec 2025 to Jan 2028). Original paper: supers 0.093-0.096, public 0.107-0.121, best LLM 0.111-0.122. A tournament leaderboard includes tool use, fine-tuning and ensembling entries.
numbers: Not verified by reading in this session. No xAI or Cassi entry facts or crowd-adjustment 0.01 figure found; that claim in SUBFIELDS.md stays unverified.
limits: Secondary snippets; values differ between paper versions (0.093 vs 0.096).
agent_relevance: Check the live leaderboard for the current gap; treat the crowd-adjust 0.01 claim as unconfirmed.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: System is well calibrated without special calibration training; standard post-hoc calibration (binning, isotonic regression) did not help. Performance varies by category, with a caution that subgroups are small.
numbers: RMS calibration error 0.42 (system) vs 0.38 (crowd) on test. Category Brier system vs crowd: Sports 0.221 vs 0.146 (crowd far ahead); Politics and Governance 0.198 vs 0.147; all categories 0.179 vs 0.149. Calibration of base models zero-shot was worse than the system.
limits: Category table read from a flattened PDF table; small subgroups noisy; authors warn against strong subgroup conclusions.
agent_relevance: Do not add a recalibration layer by default; averaging runs already helps calibration. Expect the biggest gap to crowds in fast-moving domains.
